states.gap: A's dots are squarer and heavier. Their edge pixels are #C67B79, about 95% of the #CF807E centre, where B's are #7F5352, about 60%. So each dot in A reads as a solid 6×6 block rather than a round disc, and a run of them looks more like a dashed rule than dotted ink. A also spaces letters about 1.5% wider (cell 26.0 vs 25.6 px), so the same two rows are 1664 px wide against 1638, and 'DRAFFT' ends at x≈1533 against ≈1508.
states.gapTheirs: B's letter spacing is 0.4 px tighter per cell, so the monospace line feels a little more packed. Its dot runs don't line up with the word quite as neatly: under 'Teh' the partial dots at each end start and finish about 1 px off from the glyph edges, while A's runs sit flush with the word's cells.
states.verdict: You can barely tell these apart: same dot pitch (8 px), same core colour #CF807E, same rows (y 121–126), same seven marked words, and DRAFFT left alone in both. A's dots have hard edges, so under a long word like 'definately' the soft dotted mark turns into a pink hyphenated bar that pulls the eye off the sentence. B's dots have soft, rounded edges and stay quiet, which is what a spell mark should do. A also sets the line a hair too loose.

states.name: syntax-light
states.gap: The syntax colour breaks on exactly the words spell check marks. In B, 'comittee' and 'Teh' are black (#1a1a1a-ish) where A keeps them in the noun orange its other nouns use ('draft', 'notes', 'noon'). 'DRAFFT' is black in B against A's ochre, and 'before' in 'before noon' is green (adverb or conjunction) where A leaves it black like the prepositions 'from' and 'on'. So in B, 2 of the 4 marked words on row 2 lose their Category, plus the ignored all-caps word, and one correct word is tagged wrong.
states.gapTheirs: The dots are the same in both images, measured: 6 px round dots on an 8 px period, bands at y=47–52 and y=121–126, 58 dots on row 1 and 36 on row 2. A's only real loss is density. It has a 25.6 px cell against B's 26.0, which is 1638 px of width against 1664 for the same two rows, about 1.6% tighter.
states.verdict: The red dots are the same in both, down to the pixel: same size, same spacing, same depth under the baseline, same count. So the choice comes down to what surrounds them. In B a misspelled word turns black, as if the syntax highlighter gave up on it, so the one word you most need to see in context drops out of the colour scheme the moment it's marked. It also paints 'before' as the wrong part of speech. A keeps every noun orange whether or not it's spelled right, and the dots sit under that colour without breaking it.
